section.heading: 9.4. Approximate Solutions of Differential Equations
Euler’s Method
section.paragraph: As in the case of definite integrals, there are many differential equations whose exact solutions cannot be found by using any of the available methods. Here again, we resort to approximate solutions.
Many numerical methods have been developed for the efficient computation of approximate solutions to differential equations. In this section, we will look at a method for solving the problem
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = F\left( {x,y} \right) y\left( x_{0} \right) = y_{0}$$

Euler’s method , named after Leonhard Euler (1707–1783), describes a way of finding an approximate solution of Equation (12). Basically, the technique calls for approximating the actual solution $$y = f(x)$$ at certain selected values of $$x$$ . The values of $$f$$ between two adjacent values of $$x$$ are then found by linear interpolation. This situation is depicted geometrically in Figure 13. Thus, in Euler’s method, the actual solution curve of the differential equation is approximated by a suitable polygonal curve.

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The x axis has five equidistant tick marks: x_0, x_1, x_, 2, x_3, and, x_4. From each of these marks, vertical lines rise up from the x axis, parallel to the y axis till the upper curve. The first curve begins directly above the mark x_0 with a marked point, descends to the right, concave up, reaches a low point directly above the mark x_1 and y is an unknown value. The curve then rises upward to the right, concave up, inflects above and a little to the right of the mark x_2, y is unknown, rises upward to the right, now concave down, bulges upward as it rises directly above the mark x_3, y is unknown and continues rising to the right and meet the line from x_4, y is unknown and continues into the first quadrant. The third and fourth segments have the same slope. A text approximate solution appears near the curve with an arrow pointing towards it.

figure.caption: Using Euler’s method, the actual solution curve of the differential equation is approximated by a polygonal curve.

section.paragraph: To describe the method, let $$h$$ be a small positive number and let $$x_{n} = x_{0} + nh$$ , where $$n = 1,2,3,\ldots$$ ; that is,
Thus, the points $$x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},\ldots$$ are spaced evenly apart, and the distance between any two adjacent points is $$h$$ units.

We begin by finding an approximation $$y_{1}$$ to the value of the actual solution, $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ at $$x = x_{1}$$ . Observe that the initial condition $$y\left( x_{0} \right) = y_{0}$$ of $$(12)$$ tells us that the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ lies on the solution curve. Euler’s method calls for approximating the part of the graph of $$f$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by the straight-line segment that is tangent to the graph of $$f$$ at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ . To find an equation of this straight-line segment, observe that the slope of this line segment is equal to $$F\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ . So using the point-slope form of an equation of a line, we see that the required equation is
$$y - y_{0} = F\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x - x_{0}} \right)$$
or
$$y = y_{0} + F\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x - x_{0}} \right)$$
Therefore, the approximation $$y_{1}$$ to $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ is obtained by replacing $$x$$ by $$x_{1}$$ . Thus,

$$\begin{array}{l} {y_{1} = {y_{0} + F\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x_{1} - x_{0}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{y_{1}} = {y_{0} + F\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)h} {{Since}x_{1} - x_{0} = h}} \end{array}$$
This situation is depicted in Figure 14.

image.alt: Details A curve and a line segment are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The y axis is unmarked. The x axis has three equidistant tick marks x_0, x_1, and, x_2. From each of these marks, a vertical line rises upward from the x axis, meeting the curve. The curve begins with a marked point labeled (x_0, y_0) where the line from the mark x_0 meets the curve. The curve then descends to the right, concave up and reaches a low point at (x_1, f(x_1)) where the vertical line from x_1 meets the curve. The curve then rises upward to the right concave up, into the first quadrant meeting the vertical line from x_2 along its path. Above the curve, the text Actual solution y = f(x) appears. The line segment begins at the same point the curve does, descends linearly to the right, meeting the line from x_1 at a marked point labeled (x_1, y_1), a little below (x_1, f(x_1)).

section.paragraph: Continuing in this manner, we see that $$y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}$$ can be found by the general formula
$$y_{n} = y_{n - 1} + hF\left( {x_{n - 1},y_{n - 1}} \right) \left( {n = 1,2,\ldots} \right)$$
We now summarize this procedure.

note.title: Euler’s Method
note.heading: Euler’s Method
note.paragraph: Suppose we are given the differential equation

subject to the initial condition $$y\left( x_{0} \right) = y_{0}$$ and we wish to find an approximation of $$y(b)$$ , where $$b$$ is a number greater than $$x_{0}$$ and $$n$$ is a positive integer. Compute

$$\begin{array}{rcl} y_{0} & = & {y\left( x_{0} \right)} \\ y_{1} & = & {y_{0} + hF\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} \\ y_{2} & = & {y_{1} + hF\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)} \\ & \vdots & \\ y_{n} & = & {y_{n - 1} + hF\left( {x_{n - 1},y_{n - 1}} \right)} \end{array}$$
Then $$y_{n}$$ gives an approximation of the true value $$y(b)$$ of the solution to the initial-value problem at $$x = b$$ .

list.item: Here, $$x_{0} = 0$$ and $$b = 0.5$$ . Taking $$n = 10$$ , we find $$h = \frac{0.5 - 0}{10}$$ and $$x_{0} = 0,x_{1} = 0.05,x_{2} = 0.10,\ldots,x_{9} = 0.45,$$ and $$x_{10} = 0.5 = b$$ . Proceeding as in part (a), we obtain the approximate solutions listed in the following table: $$\mathbf{x}$$ 0.00 0.05 0.10 0.15 0.20 0.25 $$\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{n}}$$ 1.0000 1.0000 0.9950 0.9851 0.9705 0.9517 $$\mathbf{x}$$ 0.30 0.35 0.40 0.45 0.50 $$\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{n}}$$ 0.9291 0.9032 0.8746 0.8440 0.8119 To obtain the actual solution of the differential equation, we separate variables, obtaining $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y^{2}} = - 2x\mathit{dx}$$ Integrating each side of the last equation with respect to the appropriate variable, we have $${\int\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y^{2}}} = - {\int{2x\mathit{dx}}}$$ or $$\begin{array}{rll} {- \frac{1}{y} + C_{1}} & = & {- x^{2} + C_{2}} \\ \frac{1}{y} & = & {{x^{2} + C} {C = C_{1} - C_{2}}} \\ y & = & \frac{1}{x^{2} + C} \end{array}$$ Using the condition $$y(0) = 1$$ , we have $$1 = \frac{1}{0 + C}$$ or $$C = 1$$ Therefore, the required solution is given by $$y = \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}$$
